idiom_name: POSIX advisory record lock (fcntl F_SETLK/F_SETLKW) per lockable file, or a lock row in a short libpq/sqlite3 transaction
implementation_notes: C has no data-access framework, so the lock manager is hand-written: either keep lock records in SQL and claim one inside a short transaction (libpq or the sqlite3 API), or serialise edits through POSIX advisory record locks, one small lock file per lockable, with fcntl(F_SETLK/F_SETLKW) as acquire and close()/F_UNLCK as release. The classic lock-record structure is still justified whenever the lease must outlive a system transaction and be visible to other sessions; SQLite cannot provide row locks at all (BEGIN IMMEDIATE takes the database write lock), so there the lock table or a file lock is the only pessimistic option.
pitfalls: Advisory file locks are owned by the process and vanish the moment it exits: a crashed worker silently loses its lease, while a hung client keeps one - a record with owner and acquisition time is what makes the lock visible and revocable.

fcntl record locks are per-process, so taking the same lock twice from one process succeeds and closing any descriptor to the file drops all of them; keep the lock fd out of generic cleanup paths or use flock()-style semantics instead.
SQLite has no SELECT ... FOR UPDATE - BEGIN IMMEDIATE is the only pessimistic acquisition there and it serialises every writer, so the lock table is advisory rather than enforced by the engine.
